Your questions, answered.

About the project & the beta

What is CARE, and who is it for?

CARE is a reading, research and writing environment for curious readers, students, teachers, writers and researchers. The current shelf centres on philosophy and related traditions. You do not need a philosophy qualification to begin.

CARE stands for Canonical Axiomatic Reduction Engine.

What am I looking at when I open a book?

The source text sits alongside saved CARE readings of it. You can move from a chapter to broader readings of the book, and follow recorded connections back towards the text.

Source is the supplied text. CH reads a chapter; CL brings chapters together; MC brings clusters together; WB considers the whole book. Available layers vary.

Does CARE use generative AI?

Yes. OpenAI language models generate the saved CARE readings and comparisons. Translations may be supplied or machine-generated; check their labels. These are interpretations you can inspect and question, and they can contain errors.

The model depends on the run. A complete model and generation history is not yet visible for every public reading.

What is an “axiom” here?

A concise claim within a CARE reading. It is a building block of the analysis, open to disagreement.

How do I check or cite one?

Select a claim, then open the Axiom viewer. Its routes and citation controls help you inspect the connected material. A route records a connection; it does not prove the interpretation.

Cite the original edition for the author’s words. If you discuss a CARE claim, identify the generated reading and keep its claim ID and available revision or link. Check and complete the reference for your citation style.

Which edition of each book is used?

Open Book info from the book’s options on the shelf. It shows the recorded edition, year, language and source link where available. Some records are incomplete; check the source edition before relying on a reference.

The 17 original works on the public shelf are in the public domain. The list below shows each supplied edition and its recorded source terms, including terms for transcriptions and electronic editions.

What are laterals and corpora?

A lateral is a saved comparison between books. A corpus brings a collection of works into a shared reading. Both propose relationships you can explore and question.

Find the published examples in Rooms → Laterals and Rooms → Corpora.

Explore laterals ↗Explore corpora ↗

What is available in the web beta?

You can explore published books, saved readings, available translations and comparisons. Tools for preparing books and generating new readings belong to the full application. Previews and full-version features are labelled.

For a walkthrough, use the Quick Guide PDF above.
